Abstract
This article discusses Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare, including their uses, difficulties, and solutions. Block-
chain technology improves EHR security, privacy, and interoperability, while smart contracts streamline supply chain 
management and administrative procedures. Blockchain verifies and secures IoT data, improving medical care and 
treatment, according to case studies. Generative AI systems like ChatGPT have transformed healthcare by personalizing 
therapy, diagnostics, and predictive analytics. AI systems can examine massive databases to diagnose diseases early, 
anticipate dangers, and personalize therapies. By providing timely information, boosting treatment adherence, and 
giving continuous support, AI-powered virtual health assistants have enhanced patient involvement. Generative AI 
has additionally enhanced medical research and drug development, cutting the time and expense of introducing new 
medicines. Generative AI and Blockchain provide safe patient data storage, high-quality AI training datasets, and efficient 
healthcare operations. Scalability, energy usage, and interoperability issues remain. Scalable Blockchain designs and 
standardized data integration and exchange protocols are suggested by this study. These technologies could improve 
medical research and therapy by making them safer, more effective, and more individualized.
Article Highlights
•	 This research contributes to the healthcare business by exploring how healthcare systems could use Generative AI, 
particularly ChatGPT.
•	 It begins by detailing how Generative AI could improve patient care, ease healthcare delivery, and aid medical research 
with its sophisticated data processing and predictive modelling and challenges in healthcare, including data accuracy, 
predictive capacities, and ethics.

1  Introduction
Blockchain and Generative AI have transformed healthcare in recent years. Blockchain technology solves data security, 
interoperability, and patient data ownership issues by handling sensitive healthcare data decentralized, securely, and 
transparently. Generative AI, like ChatGPT, can automate jobs, improve decision-making, and improve patient-provider 
communication to transform patient care, medical research, and administrative functions. The combination of these two 
technologies will improve healthcare efficiency, security, and patient care.
1.1  Context
The healthcare business stands to benefit greatly from generative AI, especially models such as ChatGPT [1]. Its promise 
rests in the fact that it can handle a number of healthcare-related tasks, including as enhancing the precision of EHRs 
and making it easier to integrate different systems. Generative AI, in particular, has several uses in healthcare [2]. Some 
examples of these include evaluating medical operations, facilitating data interchange, monitoring risk and pregnancy 
data, optimizing supply chain processes, and improving prescription medication administration. Generated AI also has 
potential benefits in healthcare contract management, provider credentialing, medical record interchange, clinical trial 
management, anti-counterfeiting, and medical billing [3]. Healthcare solutions driven by AI empower patients and 
enhance care quality by allowing them more control over their medical records and making data movement between 
healthcare facilities easier. But doctors and hospitals must take extreme precautions to protect their patients’ medical 
records from cybercriminals because of the sensitive information they contain [4]. With the use of modern technology, 
generative AI solutions can make sure that patients have control over their own data. It is well-established that AI systems 
are resilient against outside interference and errors. They are ideal for the secure management of medical data because 
to their robust access control capabilities. It is of utmost importance to guarantee the efficacy, security, and openness 
of healthcare systems in a society where only approximately half of the population holds access to healthcare for all [5]. 
Preventing inefficiencies and preserving the integrity of medical institutions requires ongoing research and develop-
ment of technologies such as Generative AI[6]. Transmitting information accurately and completely is crucial due to the 
wide variety of stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem, all of whom have unique requirements. Problems with data 
fragmentation and storage in different systems make healthcare decision-making and delivery more difficult. Artificial 
intelligence (AI) is essential for resolving these issues because it allows computers to carry out activities that have histori-
cally required human intellect [7]. Patient outcomes [8], treatment plan adherence[9], and access to care [10], especially 
for those in underserved or rural regions, could all be improved with the help of AI. As an example, ChatGPT can shed light 
on a patient’s recent diabetes diagnosis while also offering emotional support and further information [11]. Ensuring the 
accuracy and currency of medical data provided is the key difficulty for AI like ChatGPT in healthcare. Trustworthy data 
sources, constant updates, thoughtful evaluation of the delicate nature of medical information, and addressing privacy 
and security concerns are all necessary for dependable treatment alternatives and suggestions. A major turning point 
in AI development occurred during the mid-twentieth century during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project [3]. 
Recent developments in cutting-edge technologies, such as neural networks [11], genetic algorithms[10], and machine 
learning (ML) algorithms [9], have propelled AI forward. One example of an LLM is ChatGPT, which was first launched in 
November 2022 and is built on the GPT architecture. The capacity to produce nuanced, well-researched replies in a num-
ber of languages is largely responsible for their outstanding performance [12, 13]. As with previous discussions over the 
pros and cons of advanced AI technologies, academics and scientists have had mixed reactions to ChatGPT [14]. Factual 
errors, biases in training data, and security issues, like the propagation of misinformation, have all been mentioned as 
concerns [15]. But these caveats aside, AI models like ChatGPT can make writing and discussion far more efficient and 
accurate. Humans’ evolutionary and social psychology-based reluctance to change is well-documented [16]. There have 
been a lot of conversations since ChatGPT’s introduction about many topics, including healthcare and education, with a

In this research, we look at how healthcare organizations may use Generative AI and Blockchain to better manage 
EHRs and predictive analytics. We go into the ways in which smart contracts, cryptographic hashing, and Proof of Stake 
all work together to offer healthcare organizations efficient, transparent, and secure data management solutions.
1.2  Motivation
Improved patient care, more efficient healthcare delivery, and groundbreaking medical research are just a few ways in 
which generative AI like ChatGPT can shake up the healthcare sector. From data administration to patient interaction and 
beyond, it can handle it all, providing a revolutionary solution to the problems plaguing the healthcare industry today 
[23]. By utilizing AI-enabled applications, the silos of information in traditional models may be broken down and made 
much easier to access. This means that patients, healthcare professionals, and other stakeholders can have intelligent, 
efficient, and safe access to medical insights. Personalized patient care through sophisticated prediction models, better 
decision-making abilities, and more accurate data processing are just a few of the potential advantages of incorporating 
Generative AI into healthcare [24]. To completely reap the benefits while minimizing hazards like biases and misinforma-
tion, Generative AI adoption in healthcare must consider its predictive powers, data accuracy, and ethical implications. 
To make the most of AI, we must create and adhere to criteria that guarantee the trustworthiness, safety, and moral use 
of AI in healthcare. This will lessen the likelihood of mistakes, increase the effectiveness of providers, and improve the 
results for patients [25].
1.3  Contribution of the study
This research contributes to the healthcare business by exploring how healthcare systems could use Generative AI, par-
ticularly ChatGPT. It begins by detailing how Generative AI could improve patient care, ease healthcare delivery, and aid 
medical research with its sophisticated data processing and predictive modeling. The paper discusses AI’s challenges in 
healthcare, including data accuracy, predictive capacities, and ethics. It advises setting high standards and rules to reduce 
these issues. The study adds to the healthcare AI ethics discussion by emphasizing the necessity to ensure AI-powered 
solutions’ safety and reliability. Due to its synthesis of previous research and practical recommendations, this paper may 
be useful to healthcare professionals, politicians, and researchers interested in improving healthcare outcomes via Gen-
erative AI. The study promotes ethical and responsible AI use in healthcare to improve accessibility, efficiency, and quality.
1.4  Organization of the study
This manuscript aims to analyses Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare with a specific focus on data security, 
patient privacy, and predictive analytics. By narrowing its scope, it avoids fragmentation and provides a more concen-
trated analysis. By zeroing down on these specifics, the study hopes to provide a more thorough analysis that clarifies 
the effects of various technologies on medical treatment. In order to keep the emphasis on the key contributions of this 
research, other significant but shorter subjects are covered.
This article discusses Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare theory and practice. The study introduces Blockchain 
with Generative AI to improve healthcare security, efficiency, and patient care. Following this, the Context and Motivation 
sections discuss the healthcare issues these technologies address, setting research themes. The Literature Review covers 
healthcare Blockchain and Generative AI research, applications, benefits, and drawbacks. Materials and Methods include 
systematic literature review questions, data sources, search method, and inclusion/exclusion criteria. Data analysis and 
case studies support the Results chapter’s Blockchain and Generative AI healthcare uses, challenges, and integration 
conclusions. This paper then analyzes how these technologies may change healthcare and presents research and practice 
recommendations. Figure 1 illustrates the structure of the study.

2  Literature review
The recent merging of Generative AI and blockchain technology has created new prospects in healthcare, with the 
potential to change various domains. In addition to ChatGPT and other similar applications, generative AI encompasses 
a broader range of AI methods that may produce text, pictures, and predictive models that resemble human output 
[25]. This category comprises models such as GPT-4 and GPT-3. AI systems are increasingly being utilized in the health-
care sector to enhance patient care, streamline operations, and securing additional financing for medical research [26]. 
Examples such as Fig. 2 show AI-Driven Healthcare demonstrates the diverse applications of AI in the healthcare sector, 
including its potential to enhance patient involvement, treatment planning, and diagnostics.
The potential of generative AI to enhance the precision and efficiency of healthcare services is immense. AI systems 
can utilize advanced machine learning techniques to analyze vast datasets such as electronic health records (EHRs), 
medical literature, and genomic data [28]. This talent is particularly valuable in the fields of personalized medicine, early 
disease detection, and the development of novel treatment protocols [29]. AI-driven predictive models can greatly assist 
in identifying patients who are at a high risk of developing various diseases. This enables timely interventions, hence 
enhancing patient outcomes. AI’s rapid data processing and interpretation capabilities enable quicker diagnosis and 
personalized treatment programs, resulting in improved patient outcomes [30]. The authors explore the use of distrib-
uted reinforcement learning in a Federated Learning (FL) multi-disciplinary reinforcement system for COVID-19 patient 
data. They propose incorporating Blockchain Technology (BT) to improve clinical monitoring, secure communication, 
and data privacy in a decentralized manner. The proposed approach achieves high reliability and outperforms existing 
approaches, enhancing the efficiency and scalability of the reinforcement FL process in a distributed environment [31].
Generative AI is not limited to medical imaging; it is also revolutionizing diagnosis. Artificial intelligence algorithms 
possess the capability to meticulously analyze medical images, detecting abnormalities that may go unnoticed by human 
observers and providing potential diagnoses. In high-stakes professions such as radiology, dermatology, and pathology, 
this not only reduces the time taken for diagnosis but also lowers the likelihood of human error [32]. As artificial intel-
ligence (AI) assists healthcare professionals in managing intricate cases with greater accuracy and assurance, its applica-
tion in these industries is becoming progressively indispensable. Furthermore, physicians now can utilize AI-generated

The integration of Generative AI with blockchain technology can ultimately increase healthcare services in terms of

Data privacy and algorithmic biases are two principal ethical concerns highlighted by numerous studies on the appli-
cation of Generative AI in healthcare. Clinical decision-making processes are vulnerable to these biases, potentially 
resulting in adverse effects for particular patient populations. Blockchain technology can exhibit biases depending on 
the consensus mechanism employed, despite its acclaimed security advantages. For example, Proof of Stake (PoS) may 
induce disparities in wealth distribution within the network, but Proof of Work (PoW) can inadvertently create challenges 
due to its substantial energy requirements. This research aims to address these biases by examining feasible alternatives 
and their implications for equitable healthcare delivery [53].
Current research often neglects the biases intrinsic to Generative AI and Blockchain, even though these technolo-
gies possess significant potential for healthcare applications. The efficacy of AI models across demographic groups may 
be constrained due to training on datasets that inadequately represent diverse patient populations. Data from certain 
regions or population subgroups utilized in prior studies may introduce biases into the predictive models. The research 
often neglects the energy consumption and scalability issues associated with certain consensus mechanisms, which can 
impact the feasibility of implementing Blockchain architectures in extensive healthcare systems.
3  Blockchain and Gen‑AI in healthcare
Patients can use ChatGPT as a medication reminder tool to help patients continue to take their prescriptions at the right 
moments. In addition to offering information on possible side effects and drug interactions, the chatbot may send out 
timed reminders for taking medications. It is possible to create content quickly and efficiently by using ChatGPT. Fur-
thermore, it facilitates the simpler creation of engaging content that is personalized to specific groups. It is possible to 
make use of ChatGPT’s personalization features by analyzing user data and receiving personalized suggestions for goods, 
services, and information [54]. Furthermore, ChatGPT can be an important tool in the creation of customized virtual 
assistants that are customized to specific user needs. The speed with which ideas and knowledge can be obtained has 
the power to completely change business. This technology is easily designed with business systems and can provide 
data and suggestions in real time. As a result, businesses can maintain their competitive advantage and make informed 
decisions. Figure 7 depicts the features of blockchain.
Blockchain’s distributed ledger system, cryptographic hashes, consensus algorithms, and smart contracts make it 
decentralized. These components work together to give healthcare businesses a trustworthy, auditable, and immutable 
framework for managing and recording transactions. Public, private, and consortium blockchains are the most common 
blockchain systems. Each sort of blockchain has its own purposes and access controls. Blockchain technology is used 
in patient consent, EHRs, and supply chain verification in healthcare. Blockchain technology protects patient data and 
allows healthcare practitioners to access it. The possibility of unauthorized access or data tampering is reduced [6].
Blockchain technology improves EHR interoperability and safety in the healthcare industry. Healthcare providers can 
use blockchain technology to verify patient data. Each transaction is encrypted and connected to previous entries, creat-
ing an immutable record. This innovation will reduce data leaks and boost healthcare system trust. Blockchain technol-
ogy must enable secure health information exchange between patients and providers to protect patient privacy [55].
Pharmaceutical supply chains are more efficient and transparent because to blockchain technology. Blockchain 
technology prevents counterfeit drugs by documenting and authenticating every pharmaceutical transaction from 
manufacturers to pharmacies. Blockchain technology’s public ledger allows all parties to verify medication legitimacy, 
making this program vital to patient safety. Blockchain technology lowers supply chain anomalies and delays, making 
healthcare operations more efficient.
Smart contracts can automate administrative chores in healthcare using blockchain technology. Healthcare tasks 
including patient consent, billing, and insurance claims could benefit from smart contracts. Smart contracts are coded 
agreements that execute themselves. Automating these processes with blockchain technology lets doctors focus on 
patient care rather than paperwork. Because smart contracts automate and make transactions transparent, the block-
chain securely records them [56]. This further reduces fraud and errors. Many case studies have successfully integrated 
the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT). Blockchain is used to secure data transmissions by wearable devices that monitor 
patients’ vital signs in real time. Blockchain assures that remote patient monitoring data via Internet of Medical Things 
(IoMT) devices is authentic, unaltered, and available only to authorized medical practitioners. Another case study shows 
how blockchain technology tracks hospital medical supply movement. To prevent counterfeit parts or unauthorized

The Internet of Things (IoT) and the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) have also emerged as significant advancements 
in healthcare technology. However, these systems face challenges such as data manipulation, privacy issues, centralized 
processing, and security difficulties. Blockchain technology can address these challenges by providing decentralization 
to computing and storage, boosting security, and improving support for medical practitioners and stakeholders. The 
figure shows the use of blockchain in healthcare. Figure 8 shows the overview of blockchain technology for healthcare.
The healthcare blockchain uses a distributed ledger and smart contract blockchain network, consisting of patients, 
medical cloud, and healthcare providers. The industry is rapidly moving towards blockchain technology to address issues 
with current health information exchange (HIE) and personal health record (PHR) systems. Blockchain technology has 
gained attention due to its ability to resolve conflicts of interest and trust issues.
In the Industry 4.0 era, healthcare data is collected from multiple sources, including wearable sensors and applications. 
Access control and data audit are necessary to prevent tampering attacks and avoid multiple encryption techniques. 
Privacy issues can arise when patient medical information is not adequately protected. Decentralized solutions are nec-
essary to ensure quick and secure access to the growing volume of healthcare data. Mobility in the healthcare sector is 
increasing due to patients’ increased mobility and the data they produce.
Blockchain technology offers a potentially helpful solution at a time when concerns about personal data access and 
the need to address security and privacy issues are common. This is particularly crucial to remember in the context of 
electronic health care, where patient health information management systems must meet several requirements and 
still provide access by licensed healthcare providers. The development of smart-contract-based healthcare manage-
ment systems shows how blockchain’s decentralization principles may transform data administration on a large scale. 
Even though most people associate blockchain with the payment industry, particularly because of its association with 
Bitcoin. This is in contrast to the general perception that blockchain technology is only related to the payment industry.

Generic AI has transformed healthcare diagnostics and predictive analytics. Healthcare providers can detect disease 
early warning signs and predict health issues using AI. Massive datasets including patient histories and medical imag-

which enhance patient outcomes and lower healthcare expenditures. In challenging cases when traditional approaches

Generative artificial intelligence has also helped customized medical care. Artificial intelligence systems could analyze 
a patient’s lifestyle, medical history, and genetics to offer better treatments. This method improves therapeutic efficacy

Generative artificial intelligence-powered virtual health aides are changing patient-physician relationships. These 
AI-powered assistants can answer patients’ health concerns in their native language and provide personalized health 
information and prescription reminders. Patients with long-term health issues benefit greatly from 24/7 virtual health 
assistants. In this setting, artificial intelligence enables patient interaction, which improves health outcomes and treat-
ment adherence.
Generative AI is advancing medical research and drug discovery. AI can analyze massive amounts of medical studies, 
patient records, and clinical trial data to find new drugs and forecast their effects on the body. This knowledge speeds up 
drug development, reducing the time and cost of bringing novel cures to market. AI may model clinical trials to determine 
if novel medicines are safe and effective before being tested on patients. This method enhances research productivity 
and participant safety by identifying risks early on.

4  Integration of blockchain and AI
Security and authenticity of data used to train AI models is a major concern when adopting AI in healthcare. The 
unchangeable and secure blockchain technology can be utilized to store and distribute training data to solve this prob-
lem. Blockchain technology and artificial intelligence allow healthcare providers to train AI models with immutable, 
high-integrity data. They also offer data access. This feature allows us to protect patient privacy while artificial intelligence 
predicts.
Artificial intelligence and blockchain may solve patient data management. Blockchain-stored patient data can be 
analyzed using artificial intelligence to provide more tailored insights and suggestions while maintaining data integrity. 
This setup allows doctors to provide personalized treatment while protecting patient data. Blockchain technology’s 
decentralization gives patients more control over who sees their data and why.
A dependable Internet of Medical Things requires blockchain technology and Internet of Things applications. The 
blockchain, a distributed ledger that cannot be changed, may securely store Internet of Things device data. Only author-
ized users can view it. Blockchain technology combined with artificial intelligence improves the security and precision of 
IoMT data, enabling better and more dependable healthcare solutions. Blockchain technology can validate the unaltered 
data before AI models process it to ensure that AI findings are accurate and trustworthy.
There are pros and cons to combining blockchain and IoMT. Scalability is a concern because Internet of Things (IoMT) 
devices can generate massive amounts of data that can overwhelm standard blockchain systems. Blockchain’s energy 
usage is another issue for IoMT implementation. Ensuring blockchain technology works with healthcare systems is

5  Research methodology
5.1  Research design
To investigate the uses and effects of Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare, this study takes a mixed-methods 
approach, integrating a literature review with case study analysis. The research design was selected to offer a holistic 
view of the present situation while also delving into specific use cases, enabling a thorough examination of this new 
healthcare technology. Figure 10 illustrates the research design for Proposed Study.
5.2  Data collection
To make sure that we included the most recent innovations, we scoured various peer-reviewed journals, industry 
reports, and conference proceedings for data. Our main focus was on papers published during the last five years. 
Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and PubMed were the main databases utilized for the literature review. We used keywords 
like "Blockchain in healthcare," "Generative AI applications," "IoMT security," and "predictive analytics in healthcare" 
to find papers and studies that were interesting.
Data security, patient privacy, and predictive analytics were the key topics of focus, and case studies were chosen 
accordingly, in addition to the literature analysis. We can learn more about the advantages and disadvantages of 
Blockchain and Generative AI by looking at these case studies, which show how these technologies are being used 
in the real world.
5.3  Data analysis
The information gathered from the case studies and literature study was analyzed using thematic analysis. This 
approach aimed to find the most important uses and effects of Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare by ana-
lyzing the chosen research for commonalities and differences. While discussing these technologies in healthcare 
settings, recurrent themes such data integrity, interoperability, and scalability were given special focus.

6.1  Medication reminders
Generative AI and Blockchain can create sophisticated, secure drug reminder systems to improve adherence. Patient data 
on a blockchain can be analyzed by generative AI to generate individualized prescription reminders. This solution protects 
sensitive patient data and provides real-time, AI-driven warnings to assist patients stick to their drug schedules, increasing 
treatment outcomes [70].
6.2  Creating patient‑specific treatment plans
Generative AI with Blockchain can transform personalized medicine by creating patient-specific treatment plans. AI systems 
can customize treatment programs based on medical history, genetics, and lifestyle by securely accessing and analyzing 
blockchain-stored patient data. This integration improves medical precision and protects sensitive patient data [71].
6.3  Medical terminology and ideas
Generative AI models trained on massive medical text datasets can help practitioners grasp and apply complex medical 
language and concepts. Blockchain keeps these datasets private and tamper-proof, giving AI accurate and context-
specific medical insights. This tool helps turn clinical notes and EHR data into structured, actionable intelligence [72].

7  Challenges of generative AI and blockchain in healthcare
Utilizing blockchain and generative AI in healthcare presents numerous benefits, although it also entails distinct challenges. 
With the increase in transaction volume, scalability emerges as a critical concern for blockchain networks, particularly those 
employing Proof of Work (PoW). Proof of Stake (PoS) and many alternative consensus mechanisms are being explored as 
viable answers to scaling challenges, as they may reduce energy usage and enhance transaction speed. An alternative 
method to manage substantial data volumes without overburdening the Blockchain network is through off-chain process-
ing or sharding.
The substantial computational power required by various Blockchain protocols renders energy consumption a concern. 
Healthcare systems can mitigate the environmental impact of Blockchain technology by employing energy-efficient algo-
rithms such as Proof of Stake and utilizing renewable energy sources. Given that healthcare systems often rely on many 
technologies, interoperability is very essential. Blockchain technologies with traditional healthcare databases can facilitate 
data transmission more efficiently through standardized protocols and application programming interfaces (APIs). Blockchain 
and Generative AI are more appealing for widespread application in healthcare due to their potential to address current 
limitations in scalability, energy consumption, and interoperability. 
Generative AI can improve healthcare, but it poses hazards and obstacles that must be addressed. Since AI models need 
large volumes of sensitive patient data to function, data breaches and unauthorized access are major risks. Generative AI 
models may also perpetuate biases in training data, which can lead to discrimination or unequal treatment outcomes, espe-
cially for under-represented patient groups. Due to the opaque decision-making processes of complex AI models, healthcare 
providers may struggle to explain AI-driven suggestions to patients, raising ethical concerns about openness and responsi-
bility. Implement strong data security measures, provide diverse and representative datasets, and define ethical guidelines 
for healthcare AI use to reduce these dangers.
To maximize Blockchain and Generative AI benefits in healthcare, common data integration and exchange protocols 
must be implemented. HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) protocols help improve interoperability and 
keep patient data consistent across platforms. Healthcare providers, technology developers, and regulatory authorities must 
work together to produce universal yet localized standards. To facilitate secure and efficient data interchange, healthcare 
organizations must invest in such infrastructure and train people to handle data according to these rules. Standardized 
processes improve patient data management efficiency, accuracy, and security, creating a more connected and responsive 
healthcare environment.

7.1  Data privacy and security concerns
Integrating Generative AI and Blockchain with existing healthcare systems can be quite challenging due to the lack of sup-
port for these advanced technologies in many current systems. Ensuring smooth interoperability necessitates overcoming 
technical obstacles and establishing standardized protocols that can function across various platforms and systems [76].
7.2  Scalability issues
Scalability can pose a challenge for blockchain networks, especially when it comes to managing the substantial amounts 
of data that are generated within healthcare settings. With the increasing number of transactions and the growing 
amount of stored data, the Blockchain network may experience a decrease in speed and require more resources. This 
can present a significant challenge for the widespread adoption of Blockchain in healthcare systems [76].
Blockchain technology’s healthcare uses depend on scalability and energy usage. Blockchain networks, especially 
PoW networks, use a lot of processing power and energy. Healthcare, where sustainability and cost-efficiency are crucial, 
can suffer. Blockchain systems may also be constrained by transaction quantities, which hinder processing and increase 
operational costs. These reasons make large-scale Blockchain implementation in healthcare difficult. However, Proof of 
Stake (PoS) and sharding are being investigated to improve efficiency and reduce energy use. These ideas may make 
Blockchain more viable for healthcare, but more research is needed to determine their long-term effects.
7.3  High energy consumption
The energy consumption of Blockchain technology, especially in Proof of Work (PoW) systems, poses a major challenge. 
This can pose a challenge to implementation in healthcare, where sustainability and cost-efficiency are crucial considera-
tions [76]. Generative AI and Blockchain in healthcare have tremendous potential but also severe obstacles. To realize 
advanced technology benefits, these hurdles must be properly navigated as shown in Fig. 12.

Privacy-preserving techniques, such as federated learning, are effective in addressing data privacy concerns. They enable 
AI models to be trained on decentralized data while ensuring that sensitive patient information remains protected. 
Incorporating advanced encryption methods in Blockchain can provide an extra layer of security for patient data [77].

Dealing with scalability concerns often requires the adoption of cutting-edge solutions such as sharding and off-chain

of Work (PoW) to more energy-efficient consensus algorithms such as Proof of Stake (PoS). Because of this, it is more 
environmentally friendly and suited for use in settings related to healthcare [78]. To address these challenges, several 
solutions have been proposed, focusing on enhancing privacy, scalability, energy efficiency, and interoperability as

municate efficiently with one another [55].

9  Discussion
Concerns regarding scalability and energy consumption prompted the adoption of Proof of Stake (PoS) as the consensus 
mechanism, instead of the traditional Proof of Work (PoW). By employing Proof of Stake, the Blockchain network can 
scale while maintaining the security and integrity of healthcare data.
Although there are numerous benefits to integrating Blockchain with Generative AI, considerations like as scalability, 
compatibility, and data management must also be considered. Future study should explore advanced Blockchain con-
cepts such as sharding and off-chain processing to enhance scalability and compatibility with existing healthcare systems.
This section provides a thorough examination of significant case examples to reinforce the benefits of Blockchain 
technology in healthcare. The integration of blockchain with the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) for real-time patient 
monitoring is a significant application. Blockchain was employed to secure data transmissions between healthcare pro-
fessionals and Internet of Things devices utilized by patients. The Blockchain architecture guaranteed that only approved 
personnel could access sensitive information, hence avoiding data tampering and unauthorized access; this application 
markedly enhanced data integrity and security. Furthermore, the technology facilitated the transmission of real-time 
information to healthcare professionals, hence enhancing patient outcomes through the timely delivery of medicinal 
interventions.
Blockchain technology serves as a case study for enhancing security inside the pharmaceutical supply chain. Transpar-
ency across the supply chain, from production to patient delivery, was accomplished by employing Blockchain’s immu-
table ledger. This significantly diminished the probability of counterfeit drugs entering the supply chain. This example 
illustrated how Blockchain might enhance patient safety by enabling healthcare professionals to trace the source of each 
medication, so verifying its authenticity and safeguarding patients from counterfeit drugs. Blockchain has the potential 
to enhance healthcare data security, operational transparency, and patient safety, as demonstrated by these case studies.
Despite Generative AI and Blockchain’s great promise for healthcare applications, present research frequently ignores 
their inherent biases. When AI models are trained on datasets that don’t accurately reflect varied patient populations, 
their effectiveness may be limited across demographic groupings. Predictive models could be skewed if previous research 
relied on data from specific geographic areas or demographic subsets. Blockchain architectures may not be feasible for 
large healthcare systems due to the energy consumption and scalability problems linked with certain consensus tech-
niques, which are frequently ignored in the research.
Many studies on the use of Generative AI in healthcare have brought attention to two main ethical concerns: 
data privacy and algorithmic biases. Such biases have the ability to influence clinical decision-making and may 
have unintended consequences for some groups of patients. Despite its much-lauded security benefits, blockchain 
technology can display biases depending on the consensus process used. While Proof of Work (PoW) unintentionally

Blockchain and generative AI possess numerous potential applications in healthcare; nevertheless, there are also 
certain limitations and problems that require meticulous consideration. Scalability and energy consumption chal-
lenges are prevalent in Blockchain systems, potentially limiting their application in healthcare environments with 
numerous patients. Concerns around data privacy persist with AI, despite its potential to enhance healthcare decision-
making. Inadequate security may jeopardize important patient information, rendering it vulnerable to breaches. The 
intrinsic biases of AI models may impact the equity and quality of treatment provided to diverse patient populations, 
rendering ethical considerations equally crucial. Given these potential drawbacks, it is essential that forthcoming 
research rigorously examines these issues to develop solutions that reconcile innovation with the requirements of 
efficiency, equity, and security in patient care.
AI-powered virtual health aides automate everyday chores, changing healthcare and the workforce. Virtual assis-
tants can help healthcare doctors with administrative tasks, patient education, and 24/7 assistance, freeing up time 
for more complex cases. This transition may also impact worker dynamics when AI system management roles replace 
others. Virtual assistants can boost patient involvement, but they may limit personal interaction, which could harm 
the provider-patient relationship. Maintaining a balanced and successful healthcare workforce requires training 
healthcare workers to use AI tools and adapting to these roles.
10  Conclusion
Blockchain and Generative AI could improve healthcare, boosting safety, efficacy, and customization. Blockchain’s 
decentralized and immutable architecture protects patient data from unauthorized access. Healthcare systems 
become more transparent and trustworthy. Pharmaceutical supply chains and IoMT devices demonstrate AI’s ver-
satility in solving crucial healthcare issues. Generative AI has transformed healthcare with better diagnostics, indi-
vidualized medicine, and medical research. It has enabled early disease identification, personalized treatment, and 
patient interaction. Combining AI models with Blockchain improves data confidentiality, accuracy, and integrity, 
which improves healthcare outcomes.
These technologies have promising benefits, but scalability, energy consumption, and interoperability must be 
addressed to succeed. Scalable Blockchain structures, energy-efficient algorithms, and standardized protocols for seam-
less integration with healthcare systems are needed to address these issues. Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare 
demand a strategic strategy that analyzes their pros and downsides. Healthcare practitioners can increase patient safety, 
treatment efficacy, and medical research and therapeutic innovation through these initiatives. It will lead to more effi-
cient and customized healthcare solutions. This work adds to the current body of knowledge by investigating hitherto 
unexplored uses of Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare, meeting the demand for fresh perspectives. To be more 
precise, our study is on how the IoMT and Blockchain may work together to improve data security and operational effi-
ciency while allowing for real-time patient monitoring. An essential component of contemporary healthcare systems, 
this integration enables healthcare professionals to effortlessly share patient data while protecting their privacy. We have 
also discovered possible future uses, such as improving predictive healthcare analytics with Blockchain-AI frameworks. 
Not only do these findings deepen our comprehension of Blockchain and AI in healthcare, but they also provide fresh 
directions for future study in this dynamic area.

Abstract: This article discusses Blockchain and Generative AI in healthcare, including their uses, difficulties, and solutions. Block- chain technology improves EHR security, privacy, and interoperability, while smart contracts streamline supply chain management and administrative procedures. Blockchain verifies and secures IoT data, improving medical care and treatment, according to case studies. Generative AI systems like ChatGPT have transformed healthcare by personalizing therapy, diagnostics, and predictive analytics. AI systems can examine massive databases to diagnose diseases early, anticipate dangers, and personalize therapies. By providing timely information, boosting treatment adherence, and giving continuous support, AI-powered virtual health assistants have enhanced patient involvement. Generative AI has additionally enhanced medical research and drug development, cutting the time and expense of introducing new medicines. Generative AI and Blockchain provide safe patient data storage, high-quality AI training datasets, and efficient healthcare operations. Scalability, energy usage, and interoperability issues remain. Scalable Blockchain designs and standardized data integration and exchange protocols are suggested by this study. These technologies could improve medical research and therapy by making them safer, more effective, and more individualized.
